# History of preload Routing and charset Fallback

## The Two Threads in the Earliest Records

This page initially placed two issues in the same round of compatibility closeout work: one was the choice of replay modifier for HTML preload, and the other was how to handle content already received after a charset error. Both were close to HTML rewriting, but there was not enough material at the time to combine them into a single failure or a complete call chain.

The situation in the early records was simple: the page could be returned, but the subsequent replay result was "wrong". This statement did not distinguish between an incorrect address and input content that had already changed during decoding. On later review, the observation point for preload was the resource link output, while the observation point for charset was whether the original bytes were still preserved before the content was passed on for further processing. The two threads diverged here.

The first accessible entry point was `pywb/rewrite/html_rewriter.py`. What was recorded near the top of the file was:

```python
import re
import sys
from six.moves.html_parser import HTMLParser
from six.moves.urllib.parse import urljoin, urlsplit, urlunsplit
```

This set of dependencies made it an entry point for examining HTML nodes and URL construction. The history did not extend this into proof of ownership of the entire replay chain. `HTMLParser` indicates that markup parsing is involved here, while `urljoin`, `urlsplit`, and `urlunsplit` indicate that relative addresses and URL construction are worth checking here; they do not themselves explain how objects flow before and after a charset error.

## preload: Unify First, or Check the Type First

The initial working assumption was that preload merely fetched resources ahead of time, so continuing to use the generic embedded-resource branch would be simpler. This assumption was convenient when looking only at "whether the link returns a response". It deferred resource-type differences to downstream processing and also meant that the initial draft did not list `as` values separately.

Two approaches were later compared:

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> preload
    preload --> UnifiedEmbeddedResources
    preload --> Read_as
    Read_as --> js_modifier
    Read_as --> oe_modifier
```

The advantage of the unified branch was fewer local changes. The cost was that type information might not emerge until a later stage, with an unsuitable route for worker or font discovered only after the address had already been generated. The other approach reads the preload's `as` during HTML rewriting, selects a modifier up front for confirmed types, and retains the old handling for unconfirmed values. It adds branches, but exposes errors closer to the resource link itself.

The review ultimately favored the second approach. This was not because a complete preload mapping table was already available, but because the usage boundaries for worker and font were already enough to show that "treat all preloads as the same resource type" was too broad. The decision covered only the two types that could be verified: preload for `as=worker` uses the `js_` replay modifier; preload for `as=font` uses the `oe_` replay modifier. Here, `oe_` reuses the existing route for other embedded resources and does not indicate that a new font-specific endpoint was added.

The earlier investigation also listed `audio`, `video`, `embed`, `object`, and `track` together. These terms remain in the historical material because adjacent resource categories were investigated at the time. They were not recast as finalized routing decisions. Nor did this page force unrecognized or unconfirmed `as` values into `oe_`; doing so would turn "not yet confirmed" into "already decided".

One result independently influenced the trade-off: the output for worker and font preloads retained the original `cdn.example` hostname. As a result, this local adjustment changed only the replay modifier associated with each type, without also rewriting the source host. This sample supports the observation that the hostname was retained, but does not establish that all cross-origin preloads receive the same handling.

## charset: Preserve the Content, or Stop as Soon as Possible

The second thread began with an incorrect charset declaration. The response had already arrived, but the declared value could not reliably describe the content. The initial draft used the phrase "decoding failure", which could easily steer people toward "switch to a more permissive encoding and decode again". The later decision was to split the issue: first check whether replacement characters had been substituted into the input, then check where subsequent traversal stopped.

There were three approaches actually on the table at the time. Strictly honoring the declaration and stopping immediately on failure was easy to understand, but could truncate content that could otherwise still be passed to the replay layer for processing. Guessing a new charset and decoding again might allow a few pages to continue displaying, but would alter bytes without evidence. Falling back to the original bytes does not promise that the page is already readable, but first prevents the incorrect declaration from further damaging the input.

The local decision recorded on this page is the third approach: fall back to the original bytes when the charset is incorrect. This is a preservation choice, not a fix for the incorrect declaration, nor does it mean that all responses bypass decoding. Callers must still accept one fact: preserving the fallback content does not mean that HTML rewriting has completed, much less that subsequent node traversal will necessarily continue.

The unresolved issue at the time was the stopping point. A reproduction was needed using the directory structure provided by the caller, recording where the content stopped during charset detection, entry into HTML rewriting, or node traversal. If the reproduction shows only a decoding exception, without showing where the fallback content was actually passed, record only the decoding exception; if fallback to the original bytes is observed, record it only as a preservation result. The two observations cannot be combined into a "complete recovery" without intermediate evidence.

Neither strict failure nor encoding guessing was discarded as a "wrong approach". They still explain why the original bytes should be preserved. Strict failure exposes the problem quickly, but makes the input that could support later decisions disappear; encoding guessing improves apparent readability, but cannot guarantee that the archived content has not changed. The cost of falling back to the original bytes is leaving more decisions to downstream callers, which is also why it was not described at the time as successful normal decoding.

## A Consolidation Proposal Was Not Adopted

There was an idea to combine the two threads into a single HTML rewriter cleanup: first handle response content uniformly, then generate resource URL uniformly. This appeared to leave one fewer compatibility entry point and make it easier to include preload, charsets, and adjacent resource categories within the scope of the same change.

This proposal was not adopted. The preload failure occurred at the URL output route, while the charset risk arose after the input content might already have changed. Collapsing them into a single "abnormal rewriting result" would make it impossible during investigation to tell whether the wrong modifier had been selected or the content had lost its original bytes before entering rewriting. The two threads can share `pywb/rewrite/html_rewriter.py` as an investigation entry point, but they cannot share success criteria.

Another rejected simplification was to assign every preload type that was not understood to `oe_`. This would indeed reduce conditional branches, but would obscure how unknown types were used downstream. The current decision confirms only worker and font; the remaining categories stay under the old handling or pending verification until corresponding samples are available.

The charset thread likewise did not choose "if the page displays, it counts as success". If an incorrect declaration causes the decoder to insert replacement characters, a normal-looking page does not establish that the archived bytes are still intact. Conversely, preserving the original bytes may temporarily prevent some pages from proceeding, and this inconvenience was considered easier to verify than an unrecorded change to the input. The choice here is to reduce irreversible loss, not to promise that rewriting can complete for all incorrect inputs.

## From v1 to the Reviewed Version

v1 contained only two very short decisions: for now, split worker and font preloads out of the unified embedded-resource branch, and for now, preserve the original bytes when the charset is incorrect. That version put "need to reproduce the directory structure" at the end, but did not explain why this reproduction could not be replaced by an ordinary page check.

The reviewed version added a comparison of the options while retaining the early preference. Continuing to handle `preload` uniformly was a genuine working hypothesis at the time; after the worker and font results were confirmed, it was no longer suitable as the local decision, but it was not erased from the history. Similarly, "continue with HTML rewriting after a charset error" remained an inference that had once seemed plausible, rather than being retained as an established fact.

The dependencies at the top of the file were also added in the reviewed version. They help later readers start with HTML nodes and URL construction, rather than treating a path name as a complete relationship diagram. As for whether what was received after an incorrect charset was original content, partially decoded content, or a string, the history still had not confirmed this in sufficient detail; that gap remains.

The reviewed version also recorded the hostname sample separately: `cdn.example` was not replaced as a result of modifier dispatch. This prevents later readers from misreading "worker and font each select their own route" as "resource origins were also normalized in the same round".

## The Old Statements Remain, but Their Role Has Changed

"preload can be handled uniformly as an embedded resource" was the old judgment, not the later recommendation. It explains why `as` was not read immediately at the outset, and also shows that accessibility was prioritized over type correctness at the time. Once the local results for worker and font were available, this judgment had only historical value.

"Continue with HTML rewriting after an incorrect charset" was not turned into a definitive conclusion either. What is retained now is fallback to the original bytes, along with the requirement to reproduce the actual stopping point. If a reproduction shows that the content stops earlier, that stopping point applies only to that call path; if another path continues, that cannot be extrapolated to all incorrect declarations either.

"The page can be returned, but the result is wrong" likewise remains in its early context. It is enough to show how coarse the observations were at the time, but cannot substitute for the two distinct decisions. One requires checking the modifier, while the other requires checking whether the bytes have changed.

## Where to Start Investigating Now

The preload review still starts from `pywb/rewrite/html_rewriter.py`, first checking the adjacency between HTML nodes and URL construction, then using actual worker and font snippets separately to verify the output. The checkpoints are whether worker still maps to `js_`, whether font still maps to `oe_`, and whether the source hostname `cdn.example` is retained. Checking only that the request succeeds is not enough, because the unified branch may also generate an accessible address that is unsuitable for the resource type.

The charset review, by contrast, preserves the original content with the incorrect declaration and runs through the directory structure provided by the caller. Record two separate things: whether fallback to the original bytes occurs; the actual path where traversal stops. The existence of the fallback can be recorded only when the first has been observed; without the second, do not add a conclusion that traversal completed or continued.

Another interface review record is stored at DOC-17, where entity escaping URL and String timer callback are handled. It belongs to the same set of related closeout materials as this page, but does not change the two local decisions here about preload dispatch and Invalid charset Raw Byte Fallback.

# FontFace and cookie/range compatibility notes

This page originally began with a failed legacy call. The issue name first pointed to FontFace source, after which the cookie path and range length were put into the same compatibility check. The local entry point that could be found reliably was `karma-tests/wombat.spec.js`; in v_prev at the time, it was suitable for inspecting local declarations in tests, objects near the call, and adjacent locations. It was not sufficient on its own to determine which implementation it belonged to. The old record linked the issue name, call name, and file location closely. The later review still followed this trail, but did not treat the file location as the final conclusion.

## The Retained Old Judgment

> FontFace source Rewriting, cookie Path and range Length can be traced back through the same call. The old call failed; rerun it in processing order first; if the second run produces no new diagnostics, consider the main path stable.

This original wording remains in the record. It reflects the early working approach: failures were initially treated as a processing-order issue, and several checks were also placed on the same call chain. A later follow-up found that "no new diagnostics" can describe only one output and is insufficient to replace content comparisons, path records, or range declarations. Therefore, this passage can explain why things were arranged that way at the time, but it cannot serve as the criterion for determining that the migration is complete. The old judgment was not removed from the historical section, nor was it rewritten as a description of the current implementation.

## Entry Points and Batches

During migration, still find `karma-tests/wombat.spec.js` from the issue name or call name, and then continue only at the file's local declarations and call-adjacent locations. Batch 1 first locates the input and output of FontFace source; Batch 2 goes back to the area around the cookie and range response. The two batches do not share one "pass" result. Each batch must include the original sample actually used by the caller; leaving only the file path is not enough.

Batch 1 carries over only the samples and diagnostics for FontFace source. For the same input, process it once and save the rewritten content; then process the same input again, compare whether the content changes further, and record whether any new diagnostics appear. Identical results only show that this sample did not change further at this entry; they cannot be generalized to all compatible callers. If the second processing produces different content, retain both results; keep the difference in the FontFace batch, and do not recast it as a cookie issue.

Batch 2 separately carries over samples for cookie Path and range Length. First save the caller's original cookie Path, then save the path used by the replay endpoint. For the range response, also record the returned byte range and the full resource length; what is being checked here is whether the path changes with the replay entry and whether the length remains consistent with the response declaration. Even when rerunning FontFace produces no difference, this result cannot replace Batch 2's path and length records.

## Migration Order and Callers

The actual migration follows the order "local rewrite samples first, then path and range samples." This arrangement does not classify the two types of objects as belonging to the same implementation layer; it avoids having a single run of the old failed call change both sets of observations. If the caller must go through both paths, still save the individual results separately first and observe the combination only at the end. If no caller name can be referenced, the record contains only "FontFace caller" and "cookie/range caller"; no module name is added.

When switching from the old entry to the local declaration inside the file, first save the result obtained from the old call, then save the result obtained from the new entry. Results should be stored by batch; do not concatenate the old and new outputs into one continuous sample. For FontFace, compare the content before and after processing and the change between first/second processing; for cookie/range, compare the original Path, replay path, returned range, and full length. The comparison targets are different, and reusing the same failure description would obscure the actual differences.

```text
Old issue name / old call name
          |
          v
karma-tests/wombat.spec.js
(Local declarations and call adjacency)
       /                    \
      v                      v
FontFace source          cookie Path / range length
First processing -> second processing     Original Path -> replay path
Save content/diagnostics separately        Save range/full length separately
          \              /
           v            v
        Assess by the corresponding batch; return differences to the corresponding old entry
```

## Recovery When Differences Occur

Conditions for restoring the old path are handled according to the batch in which the difference appears. If a difference is seen only in the range response, return to batch cookie/range; do not reinterpret the already saved FontFace samples. If rerunning FontFace changes the content, return to Batch 1 and retain the two outputs from the first and second processing. If neither type of result can be matched to the original caller, stop at the corresponding batch, retain the path, samples, and diagnostics, and do not fill in the missing result as a success.

Here, "recovery" means reusing the original call entry and obtaining a comparable result; it does not mean merging the old and new outputs or deleting the old samples. The old entry remains valuable because it is where the failure phenomenon first appeared; the new entry is only responsible for pinning the problem to the declarations and adjacency relationships visible within the file. The current record does not provide the final call attribution for FontFace, nor does it provide numerical results showing that the cookie path or range length has passed.

## Later Addendum

The review added the entry points and ordering, but did not mark the originally unconfirmed parts as complete. `karma-tests/wombat.spec.js` remains the starting point for lookup and is insufficient to show that FontFace source, cookie Path, and range length belong to the same implementation layer. The old paragraph retains the attribution to "processing order" in order to preserve the mistaken path taken at the time; the actual migration should be based on the content, diagnostics, path, and range fields saved by batch.

# History of SVG filter and domain cookies

R2026.09 This round of consolidation brings together two issues that can easily be obscured by a single statement "there is a problem with resource rewriting": dynamic URL of the SVG `filter` attribute, and Collection-Level Domain cookie Cache. Both were reopened within the replay window, but they should not be attributed to the same cause. The former occurs when the value of a page object's attribute changes, while the latter concerns state boundaries defined by collections, domains and request paths.

The starting points for reading recorded in the initial draft are still useful. Near the beginning of `pywb/static/wombat.js`, you can locate `_WBWombat`,`FuncMap`,`res`,`value`, as well as `wb_replay_prefix`,`wb_abs_prefix`,`wb_rel_prefix`. These names were recorded at the time, with the aim of providing a place to return to during subsequent reading, not of classifying every prefix in the file as part of the implementation of SVG or cookies.

This record ultimately did not settle on the approach of "finding a common prefix". The reason was not that the two issues were completely unrelated, but that even when they appeared in the same replay session, they could fail in different ways: SVG can change the path to a replay address while dropping the fragment; a cookie can have the correct collection key without having the Path for the corresponding endpoint, or its Path can look reasonable while state is reused across collections. Reducing these phenomena to a single URL issue can ultimately yield only ambiguous success cases.

## Two hypotheses in the initial draft

According to the first hypothesis in the initial draft, anomalies in dynamic `filter` might originate in some shared URL processing. At the time this assessment was sufficient to guide code reading: the attribute value contains a resource path, and the Wombat side also has replay prefixes and local structures of browser objects. If dynamically written values do not enter the existing processing context, even a static page passing is meaningless.

According to the second hypothesis, Collection-Level Domain cookie Cache might be related to resource path classification. Replay endpoints use different modifiers, and cookies are sent according to their path scope; at the time it was necessary first to determine exactly at which layer collection names and domains were distinguished, and not assume from the page results that state was already isolated.

Neither hypothesis directly determined the decision. The former only indicates that dynamic properties are worth observing separately, while the latter only indicates that the endpoint Path cannot be ignored. They do not indicate whether the fragment of SVG is retained, nor whether the tracker key includes the collection name. The follow-up review closed these two gaps by defining explicit closure boundaries.

The initial draft also left a broad judgment: if the replay prefix is consistent on the browser side, the two items could probably be confirmed together. This statement is now marked obsolete. Prefix consistency describes how an address enters the replay representation; it does not describe whether the resource's internal target in the SVG attribute is still usable, nor which collection the cookie state belongs to. It can serve as an entry point for locating, but not as a criterion for passing.

## Reading scope starting from the beginning of the file

The local fragment of `pywb/static/wombat.js` visible in the frozen version is as follows:

```javascript
var _WBWombat = function($wbwindow, wbinfo) {
function FuncMap() {
var res = this.find(func);
var value = initter();
```

The first thing that can be confirmed here is the browser-side context: `_WBWombat` accepts `$wbwindow` and `wbinfo`, and the file contains a function-mapping structure. The mapping first looks up by function, then initializes a value when one is missing. This local structure explains why the dynamic object proxy and property changes are worth investigating near the same file.

`wb_replay_prefix`, `wb_abs_prefix`, and `wb_rel_prefix` are likewise retained only as adjacent objects. They respectively suggest that representations for replay, absolute addresses, and relative addresses have appeared near this browser-side module. For the SVG item, subsequent reading should focus on how the URL inside the attribute is handled in this context; for the cookie item, reading must return to the boundary between the collection key and the endpoint Path. The two tracks diverge here.

In an early record, someone described `FuncMap` as "possibly just filter's processing table." This wording is no longer used. The existence of the function mapping does not allow it to be directly equated with the rules for a certain class of SVG attributes. This old judgment is retained to prevent later code reading from mistakenly writing "file adjacency" as "implementation ownership."

Likewise, the three prefix variables do not constitute naming evidence for the cookie cache. A cookie is request state, while a prefix is part of the replay address representation; the two meet within the same request, but they are not interchangeable concepts. The initial draft put them in one paragraph for convenient reference, but the reviewed version needs to restore the separation between them.

## SVG branch: Property changes are not an ancillary part of initial-screen parsing

The observation recorded when item SVG was created was "abnormal state after processing by SVG filter Dynamic Rewriting". RPL-211 serves only as a navigation entry point for this branch. The card later had a sample attached and moved into active processing; the available materials do not provide the sample's full DOM, the script sequence, or the network results, so no page structure is invented here.

The current requirement for closure is: client-side Wombat will rewrite URL in the SVG `filter` attribute while preserving the original resource path and fragment identifier.

This requirement limits the issue to resource URL in the SVG attribute. Here, the fragment identifier refers to the part of URL that locates a target within the resource. For filter, changing the path to a replay URL but losing the fragment is a different failure from the entire URL never entering the rewrite process. The former is especially easy to miss in static screenshots: network requests may still occur, but the visual result no longer points to the original internal target.

"Dynamic" also does not mean running another routine check after the page loads, but rather that attribute value changes themselves must be covered by this requirement. The `filter` value in the initial DOM may be correct, yet new values substituted or written at runtime may still bypass the original processing. If only the page's initial source and final screenshot are retained, an issue that appears only after interaction or script execution will be incorrectly classified as normal.

Therefore, on the SVG side, "there are no blank areas on the page" is not used as the recorded conclusion. The visible result on the page can be affected by resource content, rendering timing, and other attributes. The adjacent values in a single attribute change need to be retained here: the attribute value before the change, the attribute value written after the change, the resource path after entering replay, and the fragment identifier. Together, they show at which step URL was changed.

Nor should these four items become four isolated checklists. The original value is used to determine where the path and fragment came from; the dynamic value is used to determine what was written at runtime; the rewrite result is used to determine whether a replay address was formed; the fragment is used to determine whether internal targeting was preserved. If any one of these points is missing, it is difficult to distinguish whether the value was already wrong before being written, something was lost during rewriting, or a discrepancy arose after it was written back to the page object.

The initial draft included the wording "dynamic filter might just be an omission involving absolute URL". This was later crossed out. Whether a path is relative or absolute cannot by itself explain the fragment, nor can it account for runtime assignment. Even if an attribute value already contains an absolute address, it is still necessary to confirm after rewriting that both the original resource path and the fragment survive in the result.

This item also does not include every syntax called filter. This observation concerns URL in the SVG `filter` attribute. There may be similar terminology or similar URL handling in CSS, but including it as well would change the original scope of this record. If new cards or samples appear later, link them separately; the current conclusion does not draw on other contexts to fill in gaps.

The SVG side ultimately adopted the attribute boundary, not the page boundary. The page is only the environment that carries dynamic values; what actually needs to be preserved is the original resource path and fragment identifier within the attribute. With the record framed this way, subsequent anomalies can first be interpreted as distinct forms such as "not rewritten", "path changed", "fragment lost", and "dynamic value did not enter processing", rather than leaving only the description "SVG sometimes behaves abnormally".

## The cookie branch: collection names and endpoint paths each have their place

Collection-Level Domain cookie Cache comes from another record. The creation description for RPL-228 requires performing the corresponding actions in a clean working directory and checking exit codes, file changes, and leftover directories. After the card entered the release category, another point remained unconfirmed: this time, the input and output remain in the resource close count. It gives no count, resource type, or sequence of anomalies, and the current record does not turn that sentence into a claim of a resource leak or of a cache that has already become invalid.

However, the card has already established two lookup forms that must be distinguished. `cookie:` is used for the cookie tracker key for collection isolation, with the collection name appended to it. `wkrf_`, by contrast, corresponds to the worker-frame replay endpoint; cookie rewriting needs to generate the appropriate Path scope for endpoints of this type.

The two serve different purposes. `cookie:` indicates where a tracker key begins distinguishing between collections. If only the domain is present and the collection name is missing, two collections dealing with the same domain may read state left by each other. `wkrf_` indicates which type of replay endpoint path the request will fall under; even if the collection key is correct, an incorrect Path may still cause the request to be sent without the expected cookie.

The Path scope here is the range of paths the browser uses to determine which requests carry a cookie. Both it and the paths visible in SVG URL use the word "path", but they mean different things. One determines whether state is carried, while the other determines how resources are addressed. Treating a resource address with a replay prefix as evidence that the cookie Path is correct conflates these two layers.

The current decision is to retain four objects: the collection, domain, tracker key, and endpoint Path. The collection name is part of isolation; the domain is still part of the boundary; the key structure makes collection isolation discoverable through lookups; the endpoint Path determines whether state can be used with the target request. Any one item appearing correct is not enough to substitute for the others.

An earlier, more convenient formulation was: "Caching by domain is enough." That formulation has been abandoned. Domains can only distinguish origin scopes, not express isolation requirements between collections. The current key semantics require appending the collection name after `cookie:`, so classifying solely by domain omits the collection dimension.

Another formulation that was considered was: "If all subresources follow the same path rules, there will be no cache cross-contamination." This was not adopted either. Classifying paths by resource type does not guarantee that tracker keys distinguish collections; conversely, including the collection name in a key does not automatically fix an endpoint's Path. Treating resource-type rules as cache-isolation rules can easily let a normal page sample mask problems in the worker-frame branch.

The resource close count in RPL-228 therefore remains under the cookie branch. It is not part of the collection key format, nor does it change the path semantics of `wkrf_`; it indicates that this review still has unexplained lifecycle observations. Follow-up material needs to allow an input and its corresponding output to be placed back in the same record before assessing the relationship between that count and the cache state. Saving only a final cookie value is not enough to show when state was established, reused, or cleaned up.

This is also why the cookie item was not closed out using the SVG sample. A page may not have triggered the worker-frame endpoint, may belong to only one collection, or may not have gone through a lifecycle sufficient to expose the resource close count. Page resources working normally is a local observation, not a complete assessment of collection-level domain caching.

## Three closeout approaches considered

The closeout comparison was not between three complete implementations, but between where three ways of documenting the issues would lead the subsequent investigation. The first was to combine the two items into "replay prefix anomaly". It was closest to the initial draft's intuition and was also the easiest to write up in a single code-reading session. The problem is that this name cannot accommodate the SVG fragment, nor can it accommodate the collection name or the resource close count. It would encourage people to first confirm that a prefix looks correct, then miss the real state boundary.

The second option is to separate them completely, treating SVG and cookie as no longer sharing any records from this point on. This approach preserves object boundaries, but loses the historical reason they were part of the same compatibility closeout window. Both items appear in replay scenarios, and both need to retain the observations recorded alongside each other at release time. If they are completely disconnected, it will be difficult to understand later why they were rechecked in the same round.

The third option is to close out each object separately and archive them side by side by release window. SVG covers only dynamic `filter` URL, original resource paths, and fragment identifiers; cookie covers only collections, domains, tracker keys, and endpoint Path; the resource close count is listed separately as an unconfirmed observation under the cookie branch. The two items can share a review time, but not acceptance criteria or failure attribution.

Adopt the third option.

This decision also avoids compiling all replay modifiers into one long table. A complete catalog of resource types would not make collection isolation any clearer, nor can it substitute for the Path semantics of the `wkrf_` endpoint. Only modifiers already directly linked to this item are retained here, to help identify the cookie path boundary for worker-frame.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> svg_dynamic
    state "SVG dynamic attributes" as svg_dynamic
    svg_dynamic --> path_fragment
    state "Paths and fragments" as path_fragment
    [*] --> cookie_scope
    state "Collection-Level Domain cookie Cache" as cookie_scope
    cookie_scope --> key_and_path
    state "Collection keys and endpoint Path" as key_and_path
    key_and_path --> close_count
    state "Resource close count pending confirmation" as close_count
```

The two starting lines in the diagram indicate parallel review targets, not that they share an implementation. The SVG branch ends at paths and fragments, while the cookie branch ends at keys and endpoint Path, and retains the still-unexplained observation of the resource close count. The diagram does not attempt to depict call order; the actual code paths still need to be read further under the respective targets.

## Focus of the review records

SVG records should retain a continuous trail of attribute information. When an anomaly occurs, it must be possible to tell whether the original attribute already contained an incorrect value, whether the dynamically written value was not passed into rewriting, or whether the rewritten result lost the original path or fragment. Only then will the same sample remain useful for making a judgment in later reviews, rather than leaving only "it looked wrong at the time".

cookie records, in turn, should retain collection names, domains, tracker key formats, and the relevant endpoint Path around state boundaries. The inputs and outputs for the resource close count should still be matched separately based on the clues left on the card. It does not need to be expanded into a set of conclusions about all connections or resource releases; for now, all that is needed is to prevent this lifecycle observation from disappearing during release wrap-up.

The two sides can use the same replay scenario while retaining their evidence in different places. SVG obtains attribute value changes and URL results from the scenario; cookie obtains collection and domain context, endpoint Path, and how state is carried from the scenario; the resource close count is responsible only for continuing to keep the unconfirmed inputs and outputs accessible for inspection. If a scenario does not cover a branch, no conclusion should be drawn for that branch.

DOC-22 documents animation polyfill Identity and service worker cache Isolation. It is neighboring compatibility material that is useful to navigate to when comparing page-side state within the same release window; its cache discussion does not replace the assessment here of collection-level domain cookies. The targets here are collections, domains, and Path, and this should not be reframed as a service worker issue just because the neighboring document also discusses cache.

## Corrections with the old wording retained

> Previous assessment: As long as the URL prefix on the Wombat side is consistent, dynamic SVG and collection cookies can be confirmed together.

Corrected. The prefix only shows that the address has been put into some form of replay representation. It does not indicate whether the fragment in `filter` is still present, whether the collection name is included in the tracker key, or whether the cookie Path for worker-frame is correct. Checking the prefix can help identify where to start reading, but it cannot replace the separate checks for the two items.

> Previous assessment: As long as cookies are stored by domain, collection-level caches will not affect one another.

Corrected. Collection isolation requires tracker keys to use the `cookie:` prefix with the collection name appended. The domain cannot be omitted from this requirement, but it is not the only distinguishing dimension. Keeping only the domain would leave room for state reuse across collections.

> Previous assessment: The resource-close count is unrelated to compatibility in this case and should be removed from the record.

Not adopted. It is not yet sufficient to establish specific causality, but it is an unconfirmed observation explicitly recorded by RPL-228 after the classification was published. Removing it would leave later readers with only static descriptions of keys and Path, without showing that lifecycle clues from this review still have not been fully sorted out.

These corrections have not changed the initial draft's intuition that the two objects should be kept separate, but they have changed what "separate" specifically means. SVG is not about page rewriting in general; cookies are not about domain caching in general. The former is bounded by resource paths and fragments in dynamic attributes, while the latter is bounded by collections, domains, keys, and endpoint paths.

## Current decision

The current decision consists of two independent requirements.

Client-side Wombat rewrites URL in SVG `filter` attributes, while preserving the original resource path and fragment identifier. Dynamically written attribute values fall within the scope of this requirement, and it cannot be considered complete merely because initial page parsing succeeded.

Collection-isolated cookie tracker keys use the `cookie:` prefix, with the collection name appended. The domain and the corresponding endpoint's Path still need to be checked together; the path branch for worker-frame uses `wkrf_`. A correct collection key does not automatically mean that Path is correct, and a correct Path does not automatically mean that collection isolation has taken effect.

These two requirements are maintained side by side, and neither serves as an acceptance check for the other. Correct paths and fragments for SVG cannot prove that cookie state has not leaked into another collection; correct cookie keys and Path also cannot prove that new attribute values for dynamic `filter` have not lost their fragments. They share only a replay compatibility window and the history of one side-by-side review.

RPL-211 retain navigation to the SVG samples, RPL-228 retain navigation to Collection-Level Domain cookie Cache and resource-close counts. If more specific DOM changes are added later, append them to the SVG branch; if count inputs and outputs are added, append them to the cookie branch. Do not retroactively present new material from one side as conclusions about the other side's implementation.

# animation Identity and Cache Isolation Proposal

This proposal retains two parallel issues, but no longer treats them as the same type of regression. The animation polyfill issue concerns the function references handed over by page scripts; service worker cache Isolation is instead a boundary issue under certain replay usage modes. Seeing them during the same round of compatibility checks does not mean they should be addressed by the same patch.

The initial version focused on `pywb/static/wombat.js`, which remains valid, but serves a narrower purpose: it is a starting point for investigating the animation identity issue, not a conclusion about where the cache issue belongs. At the beginning of the file:

```javascript
var _WBWombat = function($wbwindow, wbinfo) {
function FuncMap() {
var res = this.find(func);
var value = initter();
```

These snippets are near lines 25, 28, 42, and 46, respectively. `_WBWombat` obtains the window object and runtime information, and `FuncMap` follows immediately; the last two lines show that it first looks for an existing function association, then initializes a value if none is found. This order is enough to let us observe "an object being wrapped again" separately from "an object entering the mapping for the first time." It is not enough to prove that all animation API pass through here, so the proposal does not treat the function mapping in this file as the definitive modification point.

## The Animation Identity Track

What needs to be preserved is not whether an animation callback can run, but whether the animation function reference the page receives is still the same original object before and after proxying. In polyfill scenarios, it is particularly easy to mistake "calls work" for "interface compatibility": the caller Fang Ke can save a reference, compare references, or pass it to another piece of code that depends on object identity. Verifying only that an animation frame executes does not address these uses.

The proposed check is small in scope: when the window already has an animation function, record its original reference, then retrieve a reference through the window interface established by Wombat; repeat the same comparison with the polyfill involved. Save the comparison results separately for native and polyfill cases, rather than hiding differences behind a single overall pass/fail result. If both scenarios preserve the same reference, the function mapping does not need a special case for this. If the reference changes only in the polyfill scenario, first check when the function enters `FuncMap`, then decide whether to cache the original reference or avoid additional binding.

One approach is not being chosen here: wrap all animation functions in an extra layer, then add properties to the wrappers. This allows calls to continue, but changes the reference to a new object; for this issue, it actually increases the risk. Another approach is to bypass the existing window proxy and expose the original function directly to the page. This seems closer to preserving identity, but it would also bypass the runtime context that the window proxy needs to maintain, so it is not suitable as the default path either.

This proposal therefore prioritizes confirming whether the mapping already provides stable references, then limiting adjustments to the polyfill branches where changes actually occur. If no reference change is observed, do not add mapping rules merely because a name contains animation. The samples to retain should include only the two sets of reference comparisons for native and polyfill cases, and whether callers depend on the same object; do not mix in unrelated page-rewriting results.

## The Cache Isolation Track

The service worker cache anomaly arises from specific usage modes, and at this stage it is not assumed to be equivalent to the service worker itself failing. During checks, first document the replay scope alongside the actual entry point used: which entry point created the cache, and which entry point subsequently read content that should not have been shared, or failed to read content that was expected to be readable. Without these two consecutive observations, simply recording a "cache isolation anomaly" cannot establish whether the deviation occurred during initialization, scope determination, or a subsequent read.

The candidate approach for this track is to establish isolation boundaries based on replay scope, rather than using animation function mapping to explain caching. The proposal does not yet specify a cache key format or presuppose which client script needs to change. First require verification to cover two different replay usage modes, and re-enter one of them after each run to confirm whether previously created content is visible. If the usage modes remain independent, no additional partitioning is needed; if cross-visibility occurs, only then should the next step trace the actual entry point to where the cache is created or read.

Counterexamples must also be retained. If the differences seen on two visits come only from different archived content, they cannot be called cache cross-contamination; if content is still reused after a refresh within the same replay scope, reuse alone also does not establish an isolation failure. The isolation discussion concerns whether there is crossover between scopes that should not share content, not whether resources are fetched afresh on every page load.

RPL-229 remains a navigation entry point for this anomaly. Its description requires terminal output and workspace side effects to be retained separately, which fits this verification: the output can show what was observed at runtime, while the side effects can help confirm whether the new usage mode brought in cache-related state. Neither should substitute for the other; output without subsequent state, or state without the entry path, cannot narrow down the issue.

## Where the Two Tracks Intersect

The two work tracks may still meet at page runtime, for example when a replay entry point both passes through the window proxy and triggers subsequent service worker behavior. However, the proposal does not use "the same page visit" as a basis for attributing both to a common cause. The animation check observes function references; the cache check observes visibility between scopes. The records should place the two next to each other so that the conditions of the same verification can be compared, but give separate judgments.

This arrangement also has a migration benefit: if handling animation identity involves only the area around `FuncMap`, the cache isolation verification will not be forced to change along with it; conversely, if cache boundaries need adjustment, the animation proxy should not be rewritten along the way. Keeping the two separate means withdrawing one will not leave the other without samples that can be rechecked.

In subsequent follow-up, RPL-212 has already confirmed the responsible entry point and begun work. It should carry forward the scope investigation for animation polyfills, without folding the service worker cache symptoms into the same set of investigation findings. This proposal currently asks the investigation to answer only three local questions: which animation functions pass through the window proxy, whether reference comparisons differ between polyfill and native cases, and whether the difference can be reproduced near the function mapping. If the answer remains only "page animations work," it cannot be used to choose an implementation path.

## Order of Work

First, perform a read-only verification on the animation side. When reading the window's original references and the post-proxy references, do not add a wrapper or change the polyfill installation order. If the results show no identity change in either native or polyfill cases, stop this track rather than expanding the change surface for a preventive patch. If only the polyfill case changes, record whether the change happens before retrieval, during mapping, or after delivery; propose a local change only after locating it in one of those stages.

Then reproduce the cache issue separately. Start each usage mode from a clean state, first establish an identifiable cache state, then switch to the other usage mode to read it. Retain the entry order in the verification notes, rather than treating incidental behavior after opening two windows at the same time as a conclusion. If cross-scope visibility or absence cannot be reproduced consistently, keep the issue unconfirmed, and do not submit changes based on guessed cache keys.

Review the combination of changes only after observations are available for both tracks. An acceptable combination is: the animation fix changes only reference preservation, the cache fix changes only scope isolation, and each has an independent rollback path. It is not acceptable to put cache rules into the function mapping to reduce the number of files, nor to use cache anomalies in place of animation object comparisons.

## Withdrawal Conditions and Open Questions

The withdrawal conditions for the animation branch are straightforward: if the comparisons show that the function object is already the same before and after proxying, or if the change cannot be consistently linked to the polyfill, withdraw any proposal to add special handling around `FuncMap`. The withdrawal conditions for the cache branch are that no crossover occurs between replay usage modes, or that the observed differences can be explained by the archived content itself; in that case, do not establish new isolation rules.

Still undecided are which layer should own the specific service worker cache boundaries, and whether the anomaly in RPL-229 can be reproduced consistently. Another point to confirm is whether animation callers compare only `requestAnimationFrame`, or also save references to the cancellation function. The former can be answered by window interface samples, while the latter needs to be explicitly documented in the same set of samples. Until these points are confirmed, keep the two tracks moving independently.

# Regex Dispatch and WSGI Response Header Troubleshooting Tree

Start with the specific symptom in the regression tests. Don't collapse the two boundaries into a single "rewrite failure." This record corresponds to `pywb/rewrite/test/test_content_rewriter.py`, which was used at the time as a starting point for looking into Precompiled Regex Rule Dispatch and Invalid WSGI Response Header Recovery.

## A rule doesn't match

If the rule object has already been precompiled before entering the rewriter, first confirm that the test passes in that object, rather than a string that still needs to be compiled. Check against the test cases related to `content`, `javascript`, `dash`, `url`, `rewriter`, and `callback`, and record the actual rule type passed in, the input being matched, and the capture groups received by the callback. If it only matches after you change the input to a plain string, stop here: this means the difference is in rule dispatch or the calling convention. You can't attribute the problem to the URL result on that basis.

If the precompiled object and the string produce the same result, check whether the callback received the same set of group values. Change only one input, and keep the failing output and the text before and after rewriting. When the result is empty, first distinguish between "no match" and "a match with no output from the callback"; the next steps differ. The available material does not definitively establish where the specific callback belongs. Don't infer the implementation file or owner from the test file's location.

## Unexpected response headers

If the symptom is that a WSGI response header contains an unacceptable value, first retain the original header name, value, and exception text from the return stage. Don't delete all the headers before checking what happens; that would lose the differences needed to assess the recovery branch. Then, using the same response, check whether the exception is thrown before the headers are written, or whether the response is rejected downstream only after it has been returned. In the former case, trace the response construction path; in the latter, trace the WSGI adapter boundary.

If the recovery branch regenerates the response, compare the status code, header list, and response body, not just whether the page loads. If only the status code remains and the header values have not been retained, record it as a partial recovery; if the exception text changes but the response still cannot be returned, stop expanding the input any further. "Recovery" in the old record was only a subject of investigation, not a confirmed fix.

## Both symptoms occur

First reproduce precompiled rule dispatch on its own, then feed in an invalid response header on its own. If only the combined scenario fails, keep both individual results and the combined input, and check whether the wrapper processes the callback output again. If the individual cases also fail, follow their respective branches; don't use one failure to explain the other.

If you don't have a stable reproduction, record the test name, input text, whether the rule was precompiled, the original response header values, and where the exception occurred. Don't infer unconfirmed call edges from filenames. Further verification should still start with the relevant cases in that test file; this page preserves the judgments made at the time, and any newly returned results need to be recorded separately.

Then note `FuncMap(function, line 28)`, `res(binding, line 42)`, and `value(binding, line 46)`; these are reliable declaration anchors to return to during this round of review.

# Response Charset and URL Encoding History

This record captures the trade-offs made when wrapping up R2026.09 on two related issues: how response content declares its charset, and how page URLs are encoded using URL. The investigation started at `pywb/rewrite/html_rewriter.py`, but the file location alone does not show that the same piece of logic is responsible for both results. The record retains search leads such as `content`, `url`, `text`, `html`, `utf-8`, `utf`, and `xample.com`, showing that the investigation at the time looked at neighboring areas of content handling, URL handling, and hostname encoding.

## Recorded Decisions

At the time, the two checks were not combined into a single verdict on "whether the page works." The response charset was assessed separately using the externally visible content-type declaration and the actual text; URL encoding was assessed separately using the result of rewriting the original URL. This was because readable page text does not prove that a non-ASCII hostname in the URL has been encoded as expected; a browser accepting the URL does not, in turn, prove that the response declaration was handled correctly.

The alternative was to retain only a single page screenshot or a single overall call result as shared evidence for both compatibility checks. That approach was not adopted. It could not distinguish a problem with the content declaration from URL rewriting changing the target, nor identify whether a failure should be traced back to charset handling or URL handling. The old record therefore required inputs and outputs to be retained separately for both successful and failed cases, rather than just noting "the page opens."

## Responsibility Boundaries

On this page, `html_rewriter.py` serves only as an entry point for verification: trace changes in responses and URLs from the areas immediately adjacent to content, URL, and text handling. The public interface side can make decisions about interface examples and the output callers actually see; this page does not draw conclusions on callers' behalf about how they consume rewritten results. Both lines of observation can occur within the same request, but must still be recorded separately to avoid mistaking the result of a charset declaration for the result of URL encoding.

## Historical Position Still on Record

This page did not establish a current specification that could be followed directly, nor did it retain complete successful calls, failed calls, or field-by-field output. Judgments about "Response Charset and URL Encoding" can only be understood in the context of this historical record: it records the decision to separate the issues and the verification entry points used at the time, and cannot be used to fill in implementation details not preserved in the source code. If verification continues later, the original response and original URL should be captured first, and the rewritten text, declaration, and URL should then be saved separately; if any one is missing, the conclusion remains incomplete.

# pywb Quality Signal Desk Window Checklist

This checklist follows one window only: borrow this entry point, collect the final output, record the return time, and leave a rollback entry point through adj-pywb. ## Before starting

- [ ] First find the "caller evidence" in `docs/adj-pywb/release/pywb-quality-signal-board-short-checklist-before-window-end.md` and confirm which regression sample is being borrowed this time. If the corresponding sample cannot be found, do not fill in the gap with a similarly named page.
- [ ] Record the borrow time, expected return time, and final output to take away. Do not touch the shared cache yet; clear only your own cache, then run the entry point once more.
- [ ] If the revision actually read by the user through the original entry point differs from the recorded revision, record the first discrepancy on site; do not first merge the two contents into a single conclusion.

## During the window

1. Run only the entry point agreed for this window, and save the caller result and failing sample. If the result is empty, preserve the empty result; do not change it to "no problem."
2. Compare `archive capture` and `response-header boundary` in the output. Even after the former appears, keep the evidence in place; if the latter does not appear, stop here. Do not continue using the borrowed resource to guess which part is missing.
3. If the result after a cold start differs from the shared-cache result, store the two separately first. Clearing your own cache does not prove that the shared cache has refreshed, nor that archive capture succeeded.

If the window needs to be withdrawn, follow the adj-pywb withdrawal entry point to record the results actually observed, then remove this borrowing; do not modify the old sample.

# pywb Quality Signal Dashboard: Trade-offs for the Observed State

The discussion started with two options: continue using the "compatibility window," or separate out the "replay modifiers." Both options allow observation on the current revision, but their failure exit paths differ. Keeping them at the same layer makes it hard during review to tell whether the cache missed or replay handling in the original state had already taken a different path.

The decision is to keep the current revision without rebuilding the environment, and to separate out replay modifiers in the existing record. "Keep" here does not mean treating the current results as permanently correct; it means first preserving the state that can be checked directly. Rebuilding the environment would change the context the review depends on. Even if the results could be reproduced afterward, that would not count as the original state documented in this record. Once cache decisions and replay handling are separated, each has its own point of evaluation. On failure, check the corresponding exit path first rather than forcing both symptoms into a single cause.

The objection was not a request to remove the old approach immediately. Continuing with the "compatibility window" remains in the record as a point of comparison. Its cost is coupling cache state to the replay path, leaving no clear way to distinguish the two when differences appear. The review required this cost to remain in the record so that later readers would not see only the "split completed" result and forget why compatibility handling was not layered on further at the time. There was not enough material then to tie that cost to specific callers, so no implementation commitment is made here on that basis.

One point needs its own note: the callers using `charset detection` at the time had not been fully verified. It is related to this choice, but that does not mean it can be assumed to belong to one of the exit paths after the split. Rollback is also still unresolved, especially whether rolling back only restores the old entry point; that still needs to be checked separately. Neither issue is evidence against keeping the current revision or separating out replay modifiers, and neither can be assumed resolved in this decision.

The entry point for this record is `docs/adj-pywb/decisions/pywb-quality-signal-cache-and-origin-tradeoff.md`; the body and attachments are still maintained by adj-pywb. Pages with similar names do not fill in the original context for this record. # pywb Quality Signal Console Troubleshooting Tree

This on-call page originally addressed only one symptom: the current entry point stopped at pywb-quality-signal, and the page did not go on to show the next segment of signals. The old wording linked this symptom directly to archive capture, so whoever took over would work through the archive, response headers, and replay modifiers. Material retained later showed that a missing original record, collection not reaching that point, an unattached exit request, and gaps in permissions ownership could all make the entry point look "stuck" in the same way.

The old branch has not been deleted, because attachments and screenshots still lead people back here; however, it is no longer suitable as a standalone diagnostic sequence. Now, first establish what you have, then decide whether you can continue. Rerunning first usually replaces the first anomaly with a new run and must not be treated as recovery of the original incident.

```text
Does the current entry point retain the original record for this run?
├─ No
│  ├─ Screenshots only
│  │  └─ Mark the original request as missing; stop at sample not preserved
│  └─ Not even the states before and after the failure are available
│     └─ Export both states first, then determine whether the record can be obtained
└─ Yes
   ├─ Are the collection and execution states consistent?
   │  ├─ No: first verify whether collection/execution is enabled
   │  └─ Yes: compare against the most recent normal sample to find the first difference
   └─ Where is the first difference?
      ├─ Current entry point or environment: handle it within the signal console
      ├─ Archive capture: preserve the samples and continue to the response-header boundary
      ├─ Replay modifier: gather all required material, then hand off to the interface maintainer
      └─ Requires a change to user-visible behavior: stop and enter formal review
```

## Preserve the entry point first; do not explain it yet

At the start, keep the current entry point, the original input, the revision for that run, and the first visible state together. A normal sample is not a substitute; it is only used later to find the first difference. If only the final state remains from the incident, do not split it up to fill in the states before and after the failure; it only shows the last state read later.

Here, "original record" means the content left by pywb-quality-signal for that run, not screenshots compiled later or a new set of states generated by a rerun. Screenshots can show that the entry point was hit at the time, but may not reveal the order of the request, collection, and execution. It is fine to keep screenshots alongside the record, but not to use them to fill in the request.

The old page described additional collection as a recovery action, but that description was later narrowed. Additional collection preserves material for the next observation; the request that was not attached last time still is not attached. If the person taking over conflates the two from the outset, the tree will incorrectly jump from "no sample" to "confirmed archive difference".

Only screenshots remain from the old incident covered by RPLA-004, and the original request associated with the exit entry point was not attached. This branch should stop at "original request missing". It does not indicate that archive capture failed, nor that the replay modifier has already been executed; the on-call page only needs to retain the fact that the entry point was hit and identify the missing segment.

If the current entry point does not even have the states before and after the failure, first export both states as described in RPLA-021. If the original record still cannot be obtained after the export, keep "sample not preserved"; do not run a new, clean sample to replace it just to make the tree look complete. The new sample can be used for later comparisons, but must not be merged with the first failure.

## Collection and execution are not the same signal

Once you have the original record, first check whether the collection and execution states are consistent. The check retained in RPLA-007 is to confirm whether both sides are enabled; when evidence is missing for one side, do not treat an absent signal as zero, and do not go straight to the replay side. First indicate whether the inconsistency is in collection or execution; if no material is available at the current entry point, troubleshooting ends here.

Only when both sides are consistent should you compare against the most recent normal sample. Change only one condition in the comparison, with the aim of finding the first difference, not inferring a complete chain by working backward from average results, directory names, or the final display. The normal sample's green status can only help locate the point; it cannot establish the cause for the failed sample.

When the first difference is at the current entry point or in the environment, continue handling it within pywb · Quality Signal Board. Entry-point changes, collection state, and execution state still have not crossed the project's interface boundary, so there is no need to hand the material elsewhere just because of the word "stuck". The handoff material must specify which point is being compared, rather than merely saying "different from the normal sample".

The old records include one premature retry. After the rerun turned green, the incident was treated as recovered; the practice was later changed to prioritize preserving the first failed sample and the environmental differences. Environmental differences here are only part of the comparison conditions; they cannot replace the missing request or turn an unrecorded first run into a confirmed result.

## Narrow it down only after reaching archive capture

When the first difference falls after archive capture, preserve the failed and normal samples first, then continue to the response-header boundary. This branch only identifies where to look next; it does not directly identify the response-header boundary as the cause. The old attachments show cases where someone cleared the incident state or immediately handed it off on seeing this location, losing the first difference that the next person would need most.

If resource release has not appeared, record this as the signal not having reached that point yet. It is not evidence of a resource problem, nor can it fill the gap before archive capture. If the original record already cuts off earlier, return to the sample-not-preserved branch; do not assign both "abnormal resource release" and "missing request" as causes.

The old tree once treated all differences after archive capture as requiring an external handoff. That judgment was later revised: if the difference is still within the signal console's own collection, execution, or resource scope, the on-call person continues; only when the material clearly crosses the interface should a handoff to the corresponding maintainer be prepared. This is not intended to delay the handoff, but to avoid sending out a sample with an incomplete entry point only to have it sent back.

If the difference already points to a replay modifier, the handoff material must include at least the original input, the revision for that run, the failed sample, the normal sample, and the first difference. If any one of these is missing, return to the earlier preservation branch. Substituting "it might be replay" for this material does not narrow down the issue, nor does it let the person taking over recheck it.

## Use a separate branch for exit actions and gaps in permissions ownership

When an exit action appears but the original request was not attached, continue to treat it as a screenshot-only incident. It can remain alongside the current entry point, but must not automatically be merged into archive capture. This distinction was unclear in early versions, and someone once treated the exit-side record as a confirmed execution chain; it is now treated only as an indication that the original request is missing.

An unfilled permissions-maintainer role is another stopping point. The requirement in RPLA-014 is for the temporary assignee to handle only expiry actions, not to define the long-term implications on behalf of pywb · Quality Signal Board. If a permissions issue has already blocked export or reading, specify whether the block occurs before entry, collection, or sample comparison; do not combine the permissions ownership gap and the replay modifier into one branch.

Both things may be present at the same time: someone lacks permission to export the states before and after the failure, while the record happens to show a difference near the replay modifier. # Caller Integration Maintainer Map

This file retains the contact map from the caller integration phase, not a complete responsibility matrix for sample archive. The earliest table had only three slots: response header boundary, resource release, and preservation worker. That format gave the on-call person somewhere to route a sample initially, but put "someone is handling the situation" and "someone owns the assessment long-term" in the same column. When old samples were revisited later, blanks were often read as default ownership.

The old table has not been deleted; it remains here as originally written:

| Old object name | Old wording | What this still lets us do |
|---|---|---|
| `response header boundary` | Module on-call | Route the observed behavior to the module intake point; this does not mean a long-term owner has been confirmed |
| `resource release` | Not yet confirmed | Leave the slot blank and wait for an explicit handoff record |
| `preservation worker` | Caller to fill in a name | Ask the side still using the sample for contact information |

"Module on-call" used to be written as if it were the owner of archive capture. That wording can now only be read as a temporary intake point: if there is nowhere to send a sample, this intake point receives it first; the module maintainer still decides whether it then falls within the module's maintenance scope. The `resource release` entry did not get a name just because the table had been filled in, either. When old records are missing an intervening handoff, leaving the slot blank is more useful than filling in someone who seems plausible.

Three types of actions are now recorded separately. sample-archive-client-integration is responsible for handling integration cases; temporary handoff actions only indicate who retains materials, continues asking questions, or passes them on within a given window; exit actions record what remains after the caller stops integrating. All three types can be triggered by the same sample, but they cannot be collapsed into one answer to "who is responsible."

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    S[Caller sample] --> I[Project on-call intake]
    I --> Q{Which stage the issue is in}
    Q -->|Integration path or sample record| I
    Q -->|Archive capture or artifacts| M[Module maintainer]
    Q -->|Replay modifier scope| D[Relevant decision-maker]
    I --> T[Temporary handoff record]
    I --> E[Exit action record]
    T -.is not the same as.-> O[Long-term maintenance relationship]
    E -.retains.-> R[Last observation]
```

| Item | Recipient | Materials to retain at handoff | Stopping point |
|---|---|---|---|
| Integration feedback from a new caller | sample archive · Caller Integration on-call person | Sample in use, integration point, first visible result | Decide whether further assignment is needed |
| Path differences between adjacent revisions | Project on-call person | First point where the two paths differ | Do not compare the two runs' results directly side by side |
| Archive capture anomalies or artifact differences | Module maintainer | Sample, archive-side observations, existing artifacts | The module decides whether to include this in its maintenance scope |
| Permission, risks, or scope of replay modifiers | Relevant decision-maker | Where the modifier appears and its effect on the caller | Project intake does not substitute for technical decision-making |
| Temporary handoff actions | Project on-call person | Scope of the handoff, temporary storage location, end conditions | Remove the temporary contact when it ends |
| Caller exit | Project on-call person | Reason for exit, sample retention location, last observation | Do not fill in a technical conclusion for resource release |
| `resource release` | Blank | Known details of the situation and past contacts | Wait for an explicit handoff to a specialist maintainer |
| Contact information for `preservation worker` | Caller to provide | Sample still in use or a confirmed window | Leave blank until provided |

RPLB-001 has a narrow role. It requires starting from an adjacent revision with a working path and comparing only the first point where the paths differ. This comparison can help the on-call person decide whether to pass the sample to a module maintainer, but cannot prove that the archive side has changed. Subsequent review also flagged that the original input and the current result may not belong to the same run; when old links, old screenshots, and results obtained later are placed together, label them separately first, then decide whether to keep looking for someone.

Revalidation in the shared environment still follows RPLB-006 to the original sample-archive-client-integration entry point. Local samples are only material for diagnosis and cannot replace observations in the shared environment. RPLB-009: continue looking for the teams last known to still be using adj-sample-archive; even if the search ultimately finds that no one is using it, that only affects whether new samples can be obtained. It does not make the project on-call person the long-term owner.

RPLB-014 corresponds to missing intermediate records. The old approach used here is still to leave blanks: if there are no handoff materials between two successive records, do not invent a handoff relationship based on chronology. RPLB-017 is used to check the old entry point, the current target, and the last person to confirm it; slots left by departed staff remain blank. This makes aggregation less convenient, but avoids falsely recording the old entry point as still having a long-term maintainer.

Exit actions and resource release also used to be grouped together. That section no longer applies, but it is retained because old links still bring people here. Exit records must retain the sample and the last observation, while resource release requires a clearly established maintenance relationship with a specialist; the two may occur within the same window, but cannot replace each other. The same applies to temporary handoffs: someone having handled it does not mean someone is responsible long-term.

At handoff, one line is enough: who received the integration sample, where the materials are temporarily stored, whether they have been passed to the module maintainer or the relevant decision-maker, and whether the caller has exited or is still using it at the end. If the long-term owner has not been confirmed, leave the last field blank. Navigation still starts at `docs/adj-sample-archive/ownership/sample-archive-client-integration-current-maintainer-map.md`; the content and attachments under that path are maintained by sample archive · Caller Integration, so the old entry-point name is retained.
